questions.q: What is a nudge, per Thaler and Sunstein?
a: A subtle change that guides a choice without forcing it
A rule that removes a choice entirely
A financial penalty for bad decisions
A strong warning about risks
questions.why: Lesson 1 defines a nudge as a small environmental change that makes a good choice easier without forcing it.

questions.q: What makes a default so powerful?
a: You have to actively opt out for it not to work
It hides all other options from view
It comes with a cash reward
It is enforced by law
questions.why: Lesson 2 says defaults keep you on the preset standard unless you actively object.

questions.q: Which example does the summary give of a helpful default?
a: Automatic enrollment in a retirement plan
Automatic renewal of gym memberships
Candy placed by the checkout
A cashier asking about fries
questions.why: Lesson 2 cites automatic retirement-plan enrollment as a default that helps people save.

questions.q: How can cafeterias nudge people toward fruit?
a: By placing fruit where it is easy to grab
By raising the price of fruit
By hiding fruit behind the counter
By posting calorie warnings
questions.why: Lesson 1 says putting fruit by the register instead of candy would make people eat more of it.

questions.q: What happened when companies had to report carbon emissions?
a: Emissions dropped because rivals competed to look green
Emissions rose as reporting costs grew
Nothing changed until laws limited emissions
Companies stopped reporting entirely
questions.why: Lesson 3 says mandatory reporting lowered emissions, as firms competed to appear eco-friendly.
